Note · Badaracco — Defining Moments

4 min read1,006 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-badaracco-defining-moments.md

Canon · Cluster: Ethics & Judgment · Maps to Course 09 (Leadership & OB), E11 (Personal Operating System)

  • Source: Joseph Badaracco, Defining Moments (1997)
  • Core claim: The hardest ethical decisions aren't right vs. wrong — they're right vs. right: competing values, competing loyalties, competing visions of who you want to be. These decisions reveal and shape character simultaneously.
  • Framework — the questions (note: identity, not analysis):
  • What do my deep feelings tell me? (intuition as data, not noise)
  • Which option passes the "newspaper test" — could I defend this publicly, on the front page?
  • Which option best expresses who I am and who I want to become?
  • Which will I be most proud of over time?
  • Right-vs-right conflicts come in recognizable forms: truth vs. loyalty, individual vs. community, short-term vs. long-term, justice vs. mercy.
  • Applies when: a genuine values dilemma — not "do the right thing vs. the profitable thing," but two defensible goods that can't both be honored.
  • Breaks when: the identity/feelings framing can rationalize self-interest — "which option expresses who I am" is dangerously close to "which option I already wanted," and the newspaper test rewards what's defensible over what's right (a skilled rationalizer passes it easily). It offers little for power-asymmetric situations where the "right vs. right" framing obscures a real victim. Pair with a principled lens (Sandel's three theories, canon sandel justice) so the decision isn't purely introspective. Horowitz's "what you do is who you are" is the cultural-scale echo (canon horowitz what you do is who you are).

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — Badaracco lecture "Leadership & Ethics," youtube.com/watch?v=POyAnJFGzSg) In his own words, Badaracco draws the line the note's core claim rests on: most scandals aren't interesting because the answer is obvious — "the folks at Enron… did a lot of things that were wrong… it was clear what was right and what was wrong… for the vast majority of people there's very little value in talking about right and wrong." The decisions that actually torment serious managers are the ones where "their stomach is tightening… they're breathing a little faster… I call them right versus right problems." His sharpest case is the un-told half of the Tylenol story: after J&J had decided to pull the product, the heads of the FDA and FBI asked James Burke to leave it on the shelves so copycats couldn't "be the tail that wags the dog" and so the US wouldn't "exceed the terrorists." Badaracco: Burke "to this day still doesn't know what he would have done" — "an unambiguous conflict between right and right." That is the book's wager in the author's voice, and it lands harder than any third-party gloss.

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Badaracco's mechanism is that hard calls are judgments of character a manager must make alone, without clean rules and with too little time. In the audiobook preface he indicts the standard playbook — "follow the law, serve the shareholders, consult the company credo… do the right thing" — as "abstract and very general… they float serenely above the messy, complicated, anxiety-laden political dilemmas that managers must sometimes resolve, typically with too little time and information" (Badaracco, "Defining Moments" audiobook, youtube.com/watch?v=yjBbitgIgDI). His method follows directly: "the most successful guidance involves asking questions, not giving answers" — which is why the framework above is a set of identity questions, not a decision rule.
  • Real application (mined): Badaracco's recurring fieldwork example is the layoff-and-the-friend bind, "told four different versions of this exact same story" — a subordinate confides he's about to over-mortgage his family for a dream house, while you know his name is on the coming layoff list. As a corporate officer you owe "a duty of confidentiality"; as a friend you'd "reach out and pull [him] back"; if he's fishing, honesty says tell him. "This is not right versus wrong, this is right versus right versus right." The reddit corpus shows the same structure surviving outside business: r/Ethics's top dilemma thread on abortion (1,144↑) frames it as "How do we wage individual freedom against the rights of another existence?" — two defensible goods that can't both be honored, the poster's complaint being that everyone collapses it into right-vs-wrong.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the note's worry — that feelings-first framing can launder self-interest — shows up verbatim in training material: a Global Ethics Solutions video defines "situational ethics" as deciding "based on what's right for you at the time of the crisis," i.e. exactly how rationalization operates. So the adjacent corpus prescribes process and preparation over pure introspection. And Sandel's Justice lectures in the same cluster (Rawls' difference principle, Kant on treating persons as ends) supply the principled lens the note says to pair with — evidence the right-vs-right method needs a theory of justice underneath it, not just identity.

Rep

Take a real right-vs-right call you're facing. Name both goods in tension (e.g. loyalty vs. truth). Run the newspaper test and ask which choice you'll be proud of in five years. Note where they disagree.

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
